title: Sustainable finance versus non-sustainable finance and environmental sustainability: evidence from selected OECD economies
summary: This study aims to examine the role of sustainable finance vs. nonsustainable finance in environmental sustainability using OECD nations from 2012 to 2023. Surprisingly, the data characteristics provide a clear guide to choose an appropriate set of estimators. For instance, all variables are integrated at first difference, which compels this study to adopt the Johnson cointegration approach. In addition, to address cross-sectional dependence and serial correlation problems, this study employs the Driscoll-Kraay Standard Error estimator. To break the suspense, this study considers total factor productivity, urbanization, technology (including information & communication technology and artificial intelligence), green innovation, public‒private partnerships (PPPs), sustainability, and nonsustainable finance as environmental determinants. The obtained results remain fascinating for the specified nations. For instance, outcomes reveal an inverse relationship between total factor productivity, urbanization, and green innovations with carbon emissions. In addition, information and communication technology, artificial intelligence, and public‒private partnerships contribute to emissions. Similarly, sustainable finance (SF), including green bonds and green foreign direct investment, plays a significant role in addressing environmental issues. In contrast, nonsustainable finance increases emissions, except for financial stability and financial efficiency. Additionally, this study offers a moderate effect of SF on PPPs and green innovations, which does not support the sustainability theme. A heterogeneity view yields awe-inspiring results concerning environmental proxies, including CO2 emissions, ecological footprint, and load capacity factor. Finally, cross-country analysis describes fascinating outcomes under the proposed theme. Regarding outcomes, the present study offers imperative implications for becoming clean and green shortly.

title: Supply chain resilience research and the automotive industry: review protocol
summary: This project holds the review protocol for a two-part study of supply chain resilience (SCRES) research: a bibliometric analysis of the Scopus-indexed SCRES literature published between 2008 and 2025, and a PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review of the automotive sub-corpus, coded for how studies define, conceptualise and measure resilience, with particular attention to emerging-market contexts and to Morocco. The protocol specifies the search strategy and record counts, the eligibility criteria, a two-stage independent screening procedure, the closed codebook used for data extraction, the inter-rater reliability design and its decision rule, and the planned sensitivity analysis comparing full-text-coded studies with the whole sample. It was written before screening and coding under this protocol began. The bibliometric search was completed before this deposit, so the protocol is deposited rather than prospectively registered, and the resulting manuscript reports it as such.

title: Geopolitical risk, green finance, and corporate environmental performance: evidence from global uncertainty shocks
summary: Introduction The growing importance of sustainable finance has intensified interest in understanding how green finance contributes to corporate environmental performance (CEP). However, prior studies have largely assumed a stable relationship between green finance and environmental outcomes, giving limited attention to the disruptive effects of geopolitical uncertainty. This study examines the effect of green finance on CEP and investigates whether geopolitical risk alters the effectiveness of green finance across different institutional and industrial contexts. Methods The study uses a global panel dataset comprising 15,872 firm-year observations across multiple countries and industries. The empirical analysis applies fixed-effects estimation, moderation analysis, System Generalized Method of Moments (System GMM), and panel threshold regression. Industry heterogeneity and governance effects are also examined. In addition, machine learning techniques, including Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Regression Trees (GBRT), XGBoost, and SHAP analysis, are employed to assess predictive performance and identify the relative importance of key determinants of CEP. Results The findings show that green finance significantly improves corporate environmental performance, while geopolitical risk has a significant negative effect on environmental outcomes. The interaction between green finance and geopolitical risk is negative and statistically significant, demonstrating that geopolitical uncertainty weakens the environmental effectiveness of green finance. Panel threshold analysis identifies a critical geopolitical risk threshold of τ = 142.8, beyond which the positive effect of green finance declines substantially. Energy-intensive industries are found to be more vulnerable to geopolitical shocks than non-energy-intensive sectors. Governance quality strengthens the positive environmental effects of green finance and serves as an important resilience mechanism under uncertain conditions. Among the machine learning models, XGBoost achieves the highest predictive accuracy (R 2 = 0.72), while SHAP analysis identifies green finance, geopolitical risk, and governance quality as the most influential predictors of CEP. Discussion The results demonstrate that the effectiveness of green finance is conditional rather than uniform across geopolitical and institutional environments. The study contributes to the sustainable finance literature by introducing and empirically validating the Geopolitical Adaptive Green Finance Effectiveness Theory (G-AGFET), which proposes that the environmental effectiveness of green finance depends on geopolitical stability, governance quality, and institutional resilience. The findings suggest that policymakers should strengthen governance frameworks and design adaptive green finance mechanisms that remain effective during periods of geopolitical uncertainty. Investors and corporate managers should similarly incorporate geopolitical risk and institutional quality into sustainable investment and environmental strategy decisions.

title: Bridging criticality assessment and supply chain resilience : a structured framework for operationalizing mitigation actions
summary: Critical raw materials underpin the energy transition, defense, and digitalization, yet criticality assessments remain diagnostic: they quantify supply risk and vulnerability without prescribing how to act. This gap is addressed through a structured review, from which 139 mitigation actions across mechanisms, capability types, and disruption pathway categories were compiled, harmonized, and classified. A dependency matrix encodes 278 relationships between actions. To operationalize the resulting catalog, a five-stage decision funnel is introduced to filter it by actor-specific structural boundaries and operational readiness. The illustrative application to vehicle electronics shows that no single action is universally applicable, and the set of suitable actions varies with the actor, temporal horizon, degree of control, and disruption profile. By making actor-specific feasibility and inter-action dependencies explicit, the framework enables companies and countries to assemble coherent mitigation portfolios rather than deploying isolated actions whose prerequisites, amplifications, or contradictions remain unexamined.

title: Supply-chain-aware input–output tables: reintroducing wholesale and retail flows
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic and the Suez Canal blockage have shown how disruptions to wholesalers, retailers, and logistics intermediaries can ripple across entire economies. Yet the input–output (IO) tables commonly used to study such cascading effects abstract these intermediaries away: they record only the margins charged by traders, not the products flowing through them. We develop a method to reintroduce these wholesale and retail flows into national IO tables, using Eurostat data calibrated against Austrian trade statistics. The resulting supply-chain IO (SC-IO) tables cover 22 European countries over 2011–2020, preserve national accounting identities, and align more closely with firm-level business statistics than standard IO tables. Applied to a hypothetical disruption of food wholesaling in Austria, they yield economic loss estimates several times larger than standard IO tables. The SC-IO tables provide a building block for resilience analysis, agent-based modeling, and policy assessment of trade and logistics disruptions.

title: Digital transformation, dynamic capabilities and ESG performance: post-TCFD UK evidence
summary: Purpose This study examines how digital transformation (DT) affects environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and whether exploitative and explorative DT contribute differently under the UK's post- Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) regime. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in Ambidexterity Theory and Dynamic Capability Theory (DCT), the study constructs firm-level DT and ESG measures from unstructured annual and sustainability disclosures using a Natural Language Processing (NLP)–Entropy framework. Panel data for Financial Times Stock Exchange (FTSE)-listed non-financial firms (2020–2024) are analysed using fixed-effects regressions with firm-clustered standard errors. Mediation tests evaluate CSR and total factor productivity (TFP) as capability-based mechanisms. Findings DT is positively associated with ESG performance. Both exploitative and explorative DT exhibit significant positive relationships with ESG, indicating that ambidextrous digitalisation supports sustainability improvements. Mediation via CSR and TFP is statistically weak, suggesting that the DT–ESG linkage is not transmitted through these proxies within the study horizon and may operate primarily through direct digital mechanisms. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on FTSE non-financial firms and a five-year window, which may constrain generalisability and the detection of longer-run capability maturation. Future work should extend the time horizon, employ alternative capability measures, and apply stronger causal identification designs. Practical implications Firms can improve ESG outcomes by pursuing both exploitative and explorative digital initiatives, while policymakers can reinforce gains by strengthening disclosure quality and digital reporting infrastructures. Originality/value The study integrates digital ambidexterity and DCT, introduces an NLP–Entropy measurement approach for DT and ESG, and provides evidence from a disclosure-intensive UK setting.

title: Climate-risk narrative attention and carbon emissions: internal governance and coal efficiency as moderators, green innovation as a mitigating channel
summary: Global decarbonization hinges on corporate behavior, yet principal–agent conflicts often undermine firms’ responses to climate change. Despite growing regulatory and stakeholder pressure, managers may prioritize short-term performance over long-term environmental goals when they perceive climate risks as distant or uncertain. Building on the growing literature on corporate climate risk, disclosure, carbon performance, and governance, this study applies a principal–agent lens to examine how climate-risk narrative attention (expressed climate-risk perception, Risk)—climate- and carbon-related language intensity in annual reports, not managers’ private beliefs—relates to firm-level carbon emissions (CO 2 e) among Chinese A-share listed firms from 2011 to 2024. We document a positive association: denser climate-related narrative attention is linked to higher CO 2 e under China’s institutional setting. A principal–agent reading can organize that pattern; we do not directly test short-termism or incentive horizons. We further show that stronger internal controls weaken this positive slope (moderation), and assigned province–industry coal productivity is associated with a flatter slope in coal-relevant industries, while green patenting is positively associated with Risk and negatively associated with CO 2 e in the same year—conditional correlations, not causal mediation. The perception–emission link is stronger among firms with low digital transformation, state-owned enterprises, non-high-tech firms, and those in less market-oriented regions.

title: Blockchain-enabled strategic pathways for enhancing offshore wind energy supply chain resilience: An integrated decision-support framework
summary: Offshore wind energy projects face disruptions due to their complexity and reliance on the global supply chain (SC), making SC resilience vital for the reliable and sustainable development of offshore wind energy. Blockchain could enhance resilience through transparency, asset tracking and information security. To strengthen the resilience of offshore wind energy SCs, this study aims to apply an integrated decision-support framework for identifying and prioritizing strategic blockchain-enabled pathways. Drawing on a review of the literature on offshore wind energy SCs, resilience and blockchain applications, the criteria are specified. Then SWOT analysis is used to formulate blockchain-based strategies. The Fuzzy Stepwise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis (F-SWARA) and Fuzzy Measurement Alternatives and Ranking according to the COmpromise Solution (F-MARCOS) technique were used to rank the suggested strategies. To assess robustness, sensitivity analyses were conducted on criteria weights and expert weights and a comparison was performed using fuzzy decision-making techniques. Economic value and reduction of disruption costs, implementation and maintenance cost and traceability and visibility of equipment and data were the most important sub-criteria. Also, the strategies of developing a blockchain-based intelligent decision-making platform to increase SC resilience in disruption conditions, establishing a blockchain-based risk management and early warning system for SC disruptions and implementing a blockchain-based equipment tracking system were identified as the most significant proposed strategies, respectively. These findings provide context-specific insights that may inform offshore wind developers, policymakers, and SC stakeholders when considering blockchain investments and resilience-enhancing initiatives under resource and infrastructure constraints. • Introducing a strategic framework for offshore wind supply chain resilience. • Developing blockchain strategies in offshore wind projects using SWOT analysis. • Applying Fuzzy SWARA-MARCOS methods for evaluating identified strategies. • Robustness assessment using sensitivity analysis and comparison with MCDM methods. • Offering policy and managerial insights for resilient offshore wind supply chains.

title: Ownership Structure and FR Integrity: Evidence from a Developing Country
summary: This study examines the relationship between ownership structure and financial reporting (FR) integrity among non-financial firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange. Specifically, it considers managerial, institutional, and foreign ownership. The study adopts a quantitative design using 42 firms observed from 2019 to 2024, yielding 252 firm-year observations. FR integrity is assessed using the Beneish M-Score, and the hypotheses are tested with a probit regression model. The descriptive results indicate that approximately 30.56% of the sampled firm-years are classified as potential financial statement manipulators based on the Beneish threshold. The regression results show that managerial ownership and institutional ownership have negative and statistically significant associations with the M-Score, indicating higher FR integrity as these ownership proportions increase. In contrast, foreign ownership has a positive and statistically significant association with the M-Score, indicating lower FR integrity. Firm age is positively associated with the M-Score, whereas firm size is negatively associated with it. Overall, the findings indicate that ownership structure is associated with differences in FR integrity among the sampled firms. The results have practical implications for corporate governance and ownership arrangements in developing capital markets. The study is limited by its reliance on the Beneish M-Score as the measure of FR integrity; future research may consider alternative measures and additional ownership dimensions.

title: The Effect of Business Strategy, Profitability, Environmental Performance, and Corporate Social Responsibility on Firm Value
summary: This study aims to examine the effect of business strategy, profitability, environmental performance, and CSR on firm value in oil, gas, and coal subsector companies listed on Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during 2019 – 2023. The methode used is a quantitative descriptive method. This research employs multiple linear regression analysis using SPSS 26 stratistical software. The research sample consists of 30 companies selected through a purposive sampling technique, resulting in 91 units of research data obtained from company’s annual financial reports published on IDX. The independent variables studied are business strategy, profitability, environmental performance, and corporate social responsibility, with leverage and liquidity as control variables. The results indicate that profitability and environmental performance have a positive significant effect on firm value, while business strategy and CSR not is not significantly affect firm value.

title: Digital Finance, Digital Transformation, and Earnings Persistence in Chinese Manufacturing Firms: A Narrative Literature Review
summary: Digital finance and enterprise digital transformation are changing how Chinese manufacturing firms obtain capital, coordinate production, monitor operations, and communicate financial performance. Yet the implications of these changes for earnings persistence—the extent to which current earnings are sustained in subsequent periods—remain insufficiently integrated in the literature. This article provides a critical narrative review of scholarship on digital financial development, organizational digital transformation, financial reporting quality, and the persistence of accounting earnings, with Chinese manufacturing firms as the principal application context. Rather than treating digital finance, digital transformation, and earnings persistence as interchangeable indicators of improvement, the review differentiates access to finance, operational capability, accounting measurement, and the time-series properties of reported profit. It develops an integrative framework in which digital finance may facilitate sustained operating outcomes by relaxing financial constraints and enabling digital investment, while internal digital transformation may strengthen production coordination, working-capital management, internal control, and reporting reliability. However, implementation costs, speculative financing, technology dependence, and discretionary reporting can weaken or reverse these relationships. The literature provides comparatively strong evidence for finance–innovation and transformation–reporting links, but less direct evidence for the full chain ending in earnings persistence. The review identifies measurement issues, alternative explanations, contextual moderators, and a research agenda for future firm-level studies. Implications for manufacturing managers, financial institutions, investors, and policymakers are discussed.

title: The Dynamics Between Corporate Social Responsibility and Switching Costs in a Competitive Market
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines how switching costs influence firms' strategic corporate social responsibility (CSR) investments within a Hotelling framework. We analyze two scenarios: exogenous (psychological) and endogenous (CSR‐driven) switching costs. Under exogenous ones, we show a counterintuitive result: The firm with the higher switching costs chooses a higher level of CSR, thereby securing a larger market share. For endogenous costs, two cases emerge. When firms have symmetric baseline switching costs (unrelated to CSR), CSR and switching costs act as complements, leading to equal CSR investments, identical switching costs, and equal market shares. Under the asymmetric case, CSR complements a firm's own baseline switching costs but substitutes for the rival's. The historically dominant firm maintains leadership through higher CSR only if the gap between the firms' baseline switching costs exceeds a critical threshold. Below this threshold, the rival firm gains dominance. Finally, we show that CSR acts both as a welfare‐enhancing strategy and as a mechanism enabling profitable behavior‐based price discrimination (BBPD). Relative to the no‐CSR scenario, we show that CSR increases both consumer surplus and social welfare when switching costs are treated as exogenous. When switching costs are instead modeled as endogenous and asymmetric, these welfare‐enhancing effects are also confirmed through numerical simulations. In contrast, under endogenous symmetric switching costs, welfare improvements are conditional: There exists a threshold for the efficiency scale below which consumer surplus and social welfare increase and above which both measures may decline.

title: Managing Supply Chain Resilience under Recurrent Disruption: Capabilities, Digitalization, and Performance
summary: Recurrent supply chain disruptions require coordinated managerial capabilities, but existing research often examines risk management, digital technologies, relationships, and performance separately. This structured integrative review synthesized 30 peer-reviewed journal studies published in 2020–2025, identified through iterative searches of publisher platforms, DOI-indexed scholarly records, and reference lists. Eligibility required an explicit supply chain resilience focus and a managerial, digital, governance, or performance relationship. Study designs, nine non-exclusive capability categories, digitalization, and performance links were mapped descriptively. Sixteen studies carried survey-based method labels. Flexibility (16 studies), collaboration (15), visibility and information (14), digitalization and analytics (13), risk management (12), and adaptability (12) were prominent; these frequencies indicate research attention, not comparative effectiveness. Across empirical and conceptual contributions, digitalization was associated with resilience chiefly through information quality, earlier detection, decision support, and interorganizational coordination, subject to governance and operational response capacity. Performance relationships concerned continuity, recovery, firm outcomes, and sustainability, with cost and dependency trade-offs. The resulting synthesis-derived architecture distinguishes managerial and governance foundations, information and relational enablers, executable operational options, and performance protection. Unlike a simple capability inventory, it specifies where complementarities and bottlenecks may arise without claiming a validated causal sequence. The bounded, heterogeneous corpus does not support pooled causal estimates or exhaustive coverage.

title: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence in organic supply chains: A systematic review with insights from South Tamil Nadu
summary: Organic agriculture is growing rapidly in India, yet organic supply chains remain structurally fragmented, particularly in smallholder-dominated regions such as South Tamil Nadu. Digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising solutions to persistent challenges, including inadequate cold-chain infrastructure, limited traceability, intermediary-dependent marketing and certification workflow inefficiencies. This systematic review draws on evidence from 30 peer-reviewed and institutional publications. These sources were identified through a PRISMA-compliant search of Scopus, Elsevier, Taylor & Francis, Web of Science, IEEE, MDPI, Wiley, FAO, and government databases. The findings indicate that AI-enabled precision farming, machine learning-based demand forecasting, Internet of Things-enabled cold-chain monitoring, and blockchain-supported traceability improve production efficiency, market access and organic supply chain transparency. However, widespread adoption is constrained by inadequate rural connectivity, limited digital literacy, incompatibility between digital platforms and Participatory Guarantee System certification workflows, and weak first-mile infrastructure. This review proposes the Digital Transformation and AI Readiness Framework for Organic Supply Chains (DARF-OSC). DARF-OSC is a five-stage conceptual model that integrates Diffusion of Innovations theory with the Resource-Based View. Also, this review identifies five key research gaps and tiered policy recommendations for South Tamil Nadu.

title: CSR Disclosure and Price Discovery Efficiency in MENA Firms: The Moderating Roles of Foreign Directors and Shareholders
summary: ABSTRACT This study investigates the impact of Corporate Social Responsibility disclosure (CSRD) on the price discovery efficiency of 220 non‐financial firms listed on stock exchanges across 10 MENA countries from 2010 to 2022. We analyze how CSRD influences the speed at which new information is incorporated into stock prices. Our findings indicate that global CSRD and all CSRD components (environmental disclosure, social disclosure, human rights disclosure and employee disclosure) decrease pricing efficiency by amplifying information asymmetry. We conclude that CSRD acts as noise rather than a credible signal. Additionally, our study shows that foreign directors exert a beneficial moderating effect on the relationship between CSRD (including the overall CSRD measure and the four components) and price discovery efficiency. Finally, foreign shareholders serve as a positive moderator in the relationship between CSRD (including the overall CSRD measure, environmental disclosure component, and employee disclosure component) and price discovery efficiency.

title: Earnings Management and Financial Statement Reporting Quality of Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: This study examined the relationship between earnings management and financial statement reporting quality of Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) in Nigeria over the period 1994–2024. Specifically, it examined the relationship between discretionary accruals and accrual quality; loan loss provisions and accounting conservatism; earnings smoothing and earnings persistence; real earnings management and earnings predictability; discretionary loan loss provisions and transparency and disclosure; and income-increasing/decreasing accruals and the value relevance of financial statements. Anchored on agency theory, the study adopted an ex-post facto research design and employed panel least squares regression using a balanced panel of 17 purposively selected DMBs, comprising 527 bank-year observations. Panel unit-root tests indicated that the study variables were stationary, while the Kao residual cointegration test indicated a long-run relationship among the variables. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive relationship between discretionary accruals and accrual quality (p = 0.0081), a statistically significant negative relationship between loan loss provisions and accounting conservatism (p = 0.0130), and a statistically significant negative relationship between income-increasing/decreasing accruals and the value relevance of financial statements (p = 0.0364). However, no statistically significant relationship was found between earnings smoothing and earnings persistence (p = 0.6375), real earnings management and earnings predictability (p = 0.1083), or discretionary loan loss provisions and transparency and disclosure (p = 0.2193). The study concludes that the relationship between earnings management and financial statement reporting quality varies across the six dimensions examined among Nigerian DMBs. It recommends strengthened regulatory monitoring of discretionary accruals and loan loss provisioning, improved internal controls, enhanced board and audit committee oversight, and more transparent disclosure of accounting estimates to mitigate opportunistic earnings management and strengthen financial statement reporting quality in the Nigerian banking sector.

title: THE ROLE OF INDEPENDENT DIRECTORS IN CORPORATE GOVERNANCE IN INDIA
summary: Corporate governance is all about the system of rules, processes, and practices that guide how a company is directed, managed, and held accountable. When ownership and management are separate, it opens the door for those in control to make decisions that might not align with the interests of all shareholders. This issue is particularly pronounced in India, where many companies have concentrated ownership by promoters. In such cases, controlling shareholders can wield significant influence over management and the board. That's where independent directors come in, they're meant to act as a check against this concentration of power. The role of independent directors has evolved quite a bit in India. It first gained traction through regulations in the securities market and Clause 49 of the Listing Agreement, later making its way into the Companies Act, 2013. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) also plays a role in regulating independent directors of listed companies through the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.1 The main goal of an independent director is to bring an unbiased viewpoint to board discussions. They are expected to critically evaluate management decisions, safeguard the interests of minority shareholders, oversee financial reporting and risk management, and tackle any conflicts of interest that may arise. However, just having independent directors on a board doesn't automatically ensure effective corporate governance. The experiences of companies like Satyam Computer Services Ltd. and Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. (IL&FS) highlight the gap between merely following the rules and providing genuine oversight. This article delves into the legal framework surrounding independent directors in India, their key roles in corporate governance, their liabilities, the challenges they face in being effective, and the steps needed to enhance their substantive independence.

title: Corporate social responsibility and employee motivation: intrinsic and extrinsic pathways in Vietnamese SMEs
summary: Purpose This study aims to conceptualize corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a potentially need-supportive organizational context. This study examines how CSR-related autonomy, competence and relatedness are associated with employees’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and how these two forms of motivation are subsequently associated with perceived work performance and job engagement among employees of small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, this study analyzed survey data collected from 379 employees working in SMEs in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings CSR-specific competence and relatedness were positively linked to both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Autonomy, by contrast, was positively associated with intrinsic motivation but showed no significant association with extrinsic motivation. Intrinsic motivation was positively associated with perceived work performance, while both extrinsic motivation and perceived work performance were positively associated with job engagement. Originality/value This study advances employee-centered CSR research in an underexplored emerging-market SME context. This study offers guidance on CSR design choices that prioritize competence development and social connectedness to strengthen employee outcomes.

title: Analysis of Management Strategy, Corporate Social Responsibility and High-Profile Firm Value In Indonesia
summary: Information regarding Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) can encourage investors to make decisions that enhance firm value. Efficient risk management in operational activities further increases firm value while minimizing potential operational failures. High-profile companies show greater interest in disclosing CSR activities due to high external sensitivity and media coverage. This study examines the moderating effects of risk management and media exposure on the impact of CSR on high-profile firm value in Indonesia from 2016 to 2018. Using a quantitative approach, secondary data from 69 observations were analyzed through Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA). The empirical findings indicate that CSR has a significant positive effect on high-profile firm value. However, neither risk management nor media exposure moderates the relationship between CSR and firm value. These findings suggest that investors evaluate CSR implementation as a direct positive signal rather than focusing on risk disclosures or media coverage. Consequently, companies should prioritize genuine CSR practices to enhance corporate value, while regulators need to establish clearer standards for risk management disclosures.

title: Research on public trust repair paths of corporate social responsibility visual narratives in crisis public relations contexts
summary: In the context of crisis public relations, corporate social responsibility visual narrative has become an important way for corporations to respond to public doubt, explain responsibility relations, and rebuild public trust. Compared with written statements, audiovisual texts can transform corporate responsibility into a more perceptible narrative experience through shot organization, character presentation, scene arrangement, and emotional rhythm. Based on CSR videos publicly released after corporate crises from 2020 to 2024, visual text coding, questionnaire experiments, and statistical analysis are combined to examine the effects of visual authenticity, responsibility recognition, emotional resonance, and action commitment on public trust repair. The results show that the narrative path composed of factual explanation, responsibility recognition, and action evidence has a stronger trust repair effect. Responsibility recognition and action commitment have more prominent effects on public trust. Emotional narrative can increase viewing involvement, but its trust repair effect remains limited when responsibility explanation and remedial action are absent. These findings indicate that post crisis CSR videos should not remain at the level of public welfare display and emotional appeal. They should build a more credible visual communication path through clear factual response, visible responsibility assumption, and sustained action evidence.

title: Territorialidade yanomami versus geopolítica militar: narrativas em disputa na demarcação da Terra Indígena Yanomami
summary: Este artigo discute as narrativas em disputa durante o processo de demarcação da Terra Indígena Yanomami (TIY), homologada em 1992. O processo foi marcado pelo confronto entre diferentes concepções acerca da ocupação da região. De um lado, a reivindicação de uma área ampla e contínua para a manutenção e preservação das tradições e das dinâmicas territoriais dos Yanomami. De outro, um pensamento geopolítico-militar gestado desde a fundação da Escola Superior de Guerra (ESG) em 1949, consolidado na Doutrina de Segurança Nacional (DSN) e retomado pelo Projeto Calha Norte (1985), que concebeu a presença yanomami como um obstáculo à segurança e ao desenvolvimento da Amazônia. A partir da análise do Manual Básico da ESG, de documentos da Secretaria-Geral do Conselho de Segurança Nacional (SG/CSN) e do levantamento bibliográfico sobre as dinâmicas territoriais das comunidades yanomami, este artigo busca compreender as concepções que fundamentaram essas diferentes narrativas e analisar de que maneira foram mobilizadas ao longo do processo de demarcação da Terra Indígena Yanomami.

title: PERFORMANCE FINANCIERE A L'ERE DE LA TRANSFORMATION DIGITALE: UNE REVUE THEORIQUE
summary: RÉSUMÉ : Cet article examine les mécanismes par lesquels la transformation digitale peut agir sur la performance financière des entreprises. À partir d’une revue narrative, il rapproche les instruments du pilotage financier des changements introduits par les technologies numériques dans les processus, l’information et l’organisation du travail. L’analyse mobilise les principales approches du financement, de la gouvernance et de la stratégie afin de comprendre pourquoi des investissements technologiques comparables peuvent produire des effets différents. Elle conduit à distinguer les améliorations opérationnelles, telles que la réduction des délais ou la fiabilisation des données, de leur traduction effective en rentabilité et en création de valeur. Cette traduction dépend notamment des compétences disponibles, de la cohérence du projet avec les besoins de l’entreprise et de la maîtrise des coûts de mise en œuvre. La contribution proposée est conceptuelle : elle précise des relations à examiner empiriquement et ne mesure pas un effet causal de la digitalisation. Elle invite à apprécier les projets numériques sur une durée suffisante et à associer les indicateurs financiers à des mesures de fonctionnement des processus. Mots clés : Performance Financière ; Transformation Digitale ; Pilotage ; Technologies Numériques; Création De Valeur. ABSTRACT: This article explores the mechanisms through which digital transformation may influence firms’ financial performance. Drawing on a narrative literature review, it connects financial management instruments with technology-related changes in business processes, information flows and work organization. The discussion brings together financing, governance and strategic management perspectives to explain why comparable technological investments may lead to different outcomes. It distinguishes operational improvements, such as shorter processing times and more reliable data, from their eventual contribution to profitability and value creation. This contribution depends on employee skills, the fit between the project and organizational needs, and the control of implementation costs. The paper offers a conceptual interpretation rather than an empirical estimate of the causal effect of digitalization. It identifies relationships for future investigation and argues for assessing digital projects over an appropriate time horizon, combining financial indicators with measures of process performance. Key words: Financial Performance; Digital Transformation; Management Control; Digital Technologies; Value Creation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Reporting and Auditing: Challenges and Future Opportunities
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a game-changer in the world of financial reporting and auditing, revolutionizing the traditional methods of accounting and auditing by automating tasks, providing predictive insights, intelligent decision making, and real-time data processing. This research delves into the integration of AI into accounting systems, financial reporting and the auditing landscape, presenting challenges, governance issues and future prospects. The potential areas of the application of AI are covered, including automated bookkeeping, intelligent financial reporting, fraud detection, continuous auditing, blockchain-based assurance systems and AI-based sustainability reporting. Furthermore, the paper highlights several issues associated with algorithmic bias, transparency and explainability, cyber security, ethical implications and regulatory uncertainties in AI-powered accounting systems. In addition, the study examines key strategic implications for accounting firms, auditors, regulators, and policymakers on the use of AI, such as the importance of governance, the role of AI in human-AI partnerships, and the need for professional competency development. Moreover, the study identifies future trends and opportunities of autonomous accounting systems, generative AI, integrated ESG reporting and intelligent audit ecosystems. The results imply that AI can improve the quality of reporting, effectiveness of an audit, operational efficiency, and strategic financial decision-making. However, a balance is needed between technology innovation, ethical governance, regulatory supervision and professional judgment of humans for sustainable adoption of AI. The study offers a conceptual base for future research in intelligent financial reporting and auditing environment and also adds to the literature of intelligent accounting systems.

title: Green Bonds and Financial Performance of Commercial Banks in Kenya
summary: The study investigated the relationship between green bonds and the financial performance of commercial banks in Kenya. A quantitative research design using panel data analysis was used. The study adopted a census approach where 14 commercial banks having complete data for the period 2020–2024 were used. Secondary data was gathered from audited annual reports, financial statements, sustainability reports and publications by Central Bank of Kenya, using a structured data extraction template. Descriptive statistics (mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, skewness, and kurtosis) and inferential statistics (Pearson's correlation analysis and fixed-effects panel regression analysis) were used to analyse the data. The results showed that green bonds positively and statistically significantly influenced financial performance (β = 0.0905, p = 0.005). The results support the theoretical propositions of Institutional Theory. The study adds to literature by offering empirical evidence on the green bonds and financial performance relationship in the Kenyan banking context. The results can be used to develop policies on green finance adoption and sustainable banking. The commercial banks are urged to boost the issuance of green bonds to boost their profitability and promote environmental sustainability.

title: INTEGRATED COST-SCHEDULE AND PROCUREMENT ANALYTICS FOR CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY CHAINS IN SAUDI MEGA-PROJECTS: ENHANCING FORECASTING AND PROJECT DELIVERY UNDER VISION 2030
summary: Saudi mega-projects operate through dense networks of designers, contractors, manufacturers, logistics providers and specialist suppliers, so cost and schedule performance cannot be governed effectively as separate reporting streams. Procurement commitments shape the timing and price of resources; schedule changes alter purchasing priorities and logistics demand; and commercial variations feed back into forecast completion cost. This review develops an integrated framework for cost-schedule and procurement analytics in construction supply chains, with particular relevance to Saudi Arabias Vision 2030 delivery environment. Thirty peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 to 2025 were synthesised across artificial intelligence in construction management, project cost prediction, schedule forecasting, construction supply-chain modelling, resilience and digital-twin-enabled control. The evidence indicates that predictive value emerges when cost, schedule and procurement records share consistent identifiers, timestamps and decision horizons. Machine-learning and hybrid models can improve forecasting, but isolated accuracy is insufficient unless outputs expose uncertainty, identify drivers and trigger accountable management action.

title: Modeling national health supply chain resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa: an integrated system dynamics approach to routine healthcare and emergency preparedness
summary: Purpose This study aims to address important gaps in understanding public primary healthcare (PPHC) supply chain resilience in Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries, with a focus on the complex interactions between routine healthcare delivery and emergency response during infectious disease outbreaks (IDOs). Design/methodology/approach The authors developed a system dynamics model, the health supply chain resilience (HSCR) model, to integrate epidemiological dynamics, supply chain operations and healthcare service delivery in SSA contexts. The model simulates the effects of IDOs on the interaction between routine and emergency healthcare delivery and evaluates supply chain preparedness strategies. Three types of interventions were assessed quantitatively: prepositioning of health commodities, local sourcing strategies and healthcare workforce expansion. Findings The analysis highlights the inherent trade-offs between emergency response and routine healthcare continuity. Combining complementary preparedness measures results in stronger resilience outcomes than individual interventions. The HSCR model supports the quantification of these trade-offs and the evidence-based prioritization of investments under resource constraints. Practical implications The model informs policymakers and healthcare professionals on how to design and prioritize supply chain preparedness strategies that balance emergency response and routine healthcare delivery. Originality/value This research contributes to the existing healthcare resilience literature as a novel tool to operationalize resilience, supporting evidence-based decision-making for health system stakeholders. It bridges theoretical and practical approaches to resilience-building in SSA national healthcare systems, offering a replicable model adaptable to diverse disease profiles and country settings, such as low- and middle-income countries with centralized PPHC systems.

title: UN SDG WITHIN CONTEMPORARY CORPORATE FINANCE: THE GAP BETWEEN DISCLOSURE AND CAPITAL ALLOCATION
summary: Problem setting. A decade after the adoption of the 2030 Agenda, companies have embedded sustainability principles into mainstream corporate reporting, while the financial effects of this transition remain considerably less certain. The growing financing needs associated with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), together with the recent weakening of several sustainable finance indicators, make it increasingly important to distinguish between declared corporate commitment and actual capital allocation. Aim. This study aims to assess this divergence, focusing on the relationship between SDG-related corporate commitments and observable financing and investment outcomes in contemporary corporate finance. Methodology. The study applies documentary, comparative, and structural-dynamic analysis to aggregate open-source data for 2015-2025 and examines five interconnected layers, namely, corporate disclosure, labelled debt issuance, sustainable fund flows, pricing signals, and real investment. Results. The results show that sustainability reporting has become near-universal among the world’s largest companies – 96% of the G250 report on sustainability; among G250 companies that report on sustainability or ESG matters, 74% use the SDGs. At the same time, sustainable bond issuance declined by 19% in 2025 to approximately USD 866 billion, while total global bond issuance increased by almost 11% to more than USD 10 trillion. Sustainable funds recorded USD 84 billion in net outflows in 2025, while SDG-related FDI in developing economies fell by 26% in 2024. Annual labelled issuance is equivalent in scale to approximately 20-25% of the estimated USD 4 trillion annual SDG financing gap, although this comparison does not measure actual gap coverage. The findings demonstrate a descriptive divergence between mature sustainability communication and several downstream indicators of financing and investment. Practical value. This study demonstrates that corporate treasurers, investors, regulators, and development finance institutions should assess disclosure, labelled instruments, investor commitments, and real investment separately when evaluating the financial contribution of business to the SDGs.

title: How Does Downstream Customer SRDI “Little Giant” Certification Drive Supply Chain Diversification Among Upstream Suppliers? Evidence from China
summary: Growing uncertainty in the external environment has heightened concerns about supply chain security and resilience. Existing studies mainly examine the effects of China’s Specialized, Refined, Distinctive, and Innovative (SRDI) “Little Giant” certification on certified firms themselves, while its implications for the supply chain configuration of connected firms remain less understood. Using the staggered timing of certification, this study uses customer–supplier relationship data from Chinese listed firms over the period 2012–2025 and employs a staggered difference-in-differences model to examine whether downstream customer certification is associated with changes in supply chain diversification among upstream suppliers. The results show that “Little Giant” certification significantly reduces the concentration of upstream suppliers’ major trading relationships, leading to a more dispersed distribution of transaction shares across major partners. This finding remains stable across a range of alternative specifications, while an interaction-weighted event-study analysis provides complementary evidence on heterogeneous treatment timing and dynamic patterns. The mechanism analysis provides suggestive evidence consistent with a reputation-related channel and operating-resource adjustment: certified customers are associated with greater positive media exposure for their suppliers and higher operating working capital investment, while changes in current assets provide complementary evidence of operating-resource adjustment. Further analysis indicates that the estimated association is more evident in procurement relationships than in sales relationships, although the difference between the two estimates is not statistically significant. The estimated association also tends to be stronger among suppliers that exhibited overinvestment before certification and those with larger pre-certification market shares. These findings extend research on the economic consequences of SRDI certification from certified firms to their supply chain partners and suggest that firm-targeted industrial policy may be associated with cross-firm adjustments in major trading relationships through existing customer–supplier linkages.

title: Forward-Looking Financial Reporting Risk Screening in Saudi Listed Firms: Evidence from the Beneish M-Score and Explainable Machine Learning
summary: Most applications of the Beneish M-Score are contemporaneous: they screen financial statements after a reporting year has ended. This study asks whether the eight Beneish indicators measured in year t contain information about the following year's Beneish screening classification. The analysis uses a balanced panel of 66 Saudi listed non-financial firms from 2018 to 2025, yielding 528 annual financial statements and 462 M-Score observations for 2019-2025. Under the primary M > -1.78 rule, 66 of 462 firm-years (14.3%) generate a screening signal. On the untouched 2025 holdout, logistic regression achieves ROC-AUC = 0.718 and average precision = 0.371, while Random Forest achieves ROC-AUC = 0.684 and average precision = 0.406 and produces the higher precision and F1 at the pre-specified 0.50 decision-score threshold. A rolling-origin stability analysis across 2021-2025 uses the continuous current-year M-Score as the benchmark: pooled ROC-AUC is 0.537 for M_t, 0.661 for logistic regression, and 0.653 for Random Forest. Firm-cluster bootstrap inference indicates that both fitted models improve discrimination relative to M_t, whereas their difference is not statistically distinguishable. Unweighted refits produce similar ranking performance. SHAP identifies TATA as the leading Random Forest feature, followed by DEPI, AQI, and DSRI. The evidence supports explainable machine learning as a complementary prioritization tool rather than a calibrated fraud probability or a substitute for professional review.

title: Evolution Trends of Urban–Rural Logistics Convergence Development in China Against the Background of Digital Economy
summary: The convergence development of urban–rural logistics is of great significance for narrowing the divide and promoting the exchange between urban and rural areas. The digital economy has emerged as an effective pathway to break down the industrial boundaries and drive high-quality convergence of urban–rural logistics. This study analyzes the driving mechanisms and indicator system for urban–rural logistics convergence in the digital economy context, and establishes a convergence development model, an entropy weight model, and a grey relational model. Based on statistical data from 2003 to 2022, it conducts an empirical study on the convergence level, evolutionary trends, and related factors of China’s urban–rural logistics, and explores convergence countermeasures from the composite system perspective. The findings indicate that, over the 20-year study period, China has achieved tangible progress in urban–rural logistics convergence, the subsystem’s orderly development levels alternately increased, and the composite system’s convergence level steadily improved. However, the coupling intensity of urban–rural logistics remained stagnant, and disparities in orderly development continued to exist. Among the factors, rural logistics infrastructure, urban logistics value creation, and urban logistics informatization level had relatively high relational degrees with convergence development. Urban–rural logistics convergence is a systematic project; the development of the digital economy should be taken as an opportunity, and countermeasures for convergence development should be explored from four aspects: the urban–rural logistics composite system, the urban logistics subsystem, the rural logistics subsystem, and the external environment.

title: Trade Competitiveness and Market Dynamics of U.S. Eggplant Production
summary: This study provides a comprehensive economic assessment of supply, demand, and trade competitiveness in the U.S. eggplant (Solanum melongena L.) sector, using annual import and export data from 2000 to 2022. Although eggplant is a regionally important specialty crop in the United States, domestic production remains limited relative to rising consumer demand driven by demographic diversification and shifting dietary preferences. Using descriptive statistics, compound annual growth rates, correlation analysis, log-linear elasticity models, and multiple trade competitiveness indicators, this research examines long-term trends in trade quantity, value, and pricing; evaluates the responsiveness of trade flows to price changes; and analyzes the structural factors underlying persistent import dependence. Results show that both import and export quantities and values have increased steadily, with import volumes averaging nearly four times those of exports. Strong positive correlations among trade variables indicate a high degree of integration with global markets. Elasticity estimates reveal atypical positive price responsiveness in both imports and exports, indicating supply-driven price dynamics, limited substitutability, and quality-differentiated export behavior. Competitiveness indicators, particularly the consistently negative Trade Balance Index, high Import Dependency Ratio, and low Self-Sufficiency Ratio, confirm that the U.S. eggplant market is structurally reliant on foreign supply, despite the premium pricing of U.S. exports. The findings align with comparative advantage theory, market integration frameworks, and product differentiation models, showing that trade patterns are shaped by deep-rooted economic conditions rather than short-term fluctuations. This study highlights the need for strategies to enhance domestic production capacity, improve supply chain resilience, and strengthen competitive positioning in global fresh vegetable markets.

title: More Trade, Less Vulnerability? External Economic Resilience within the Expanded BRICS+ Group
summary: With the expansion of the group comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (BRICS) to eleven full members, its economic reach and, at the same time, the heterogeneity of its trade structures have increased. This paper examines whether greater trade integration within BRICS+ reduces the members’ external economic vulnerability or primarily redistributes existing dependencies within the group. Methodologically, a structured, mechanism-oriented narrative literature review is conducted using published secondary statistics and carefully selected empirical studies on trade and resilience research. The focus is on publications from 2023 to 2026. Analytically, trade integration, structural exposure, adaptive capacity, and observed resilience are distinguished. Firstly, the results show a sharp rise in intra-BRICS merchandise exports among the ten countries considered by UNCTAD, from US$84.2 billion in 2003 to US$1.17 trillion in 2024. Secondly, there are significant differences in terms of relative trade dependence, reliance on primary commodities, and the structure of technology exports. Thirdly, the Russian and South African cases demonstrate that trade reorientation can be accompanied by greater concentration of trading partners or persistent bilateral imbalances, respectively. International research on resilience further shows that concentration only becomes a critical dependency when combined with economic significance, low substitutability, and the nature of the shock. Greater intra-BRICS+ integration is therefore not generally synonymous with higher resilience. Gains in resilience are plausible if additional trade relations actually create viable sourcing and sales alternatives. If, on the other hand, concentration on individual members or products increases, this tends to represent a geographical shift in dependency. This paper thus links the BRICS trade literature with research on supply chain resilience and geo-economic fragmentation, and derives four testable propositions for future comparative analyses.

title: Sustainable Management and ESG: Integrating Environmental, Social, and Governance Practices into Corporate Strategy
summary: The use of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) factors has shifted from being a niche topic in corporate responsibility to becoming a much more prominent role in strategic management, risk governance, investment analysis and organizational accountability. This paper explores the potential of applying ESG principles to the company's strategy to achieve sustainable management and long-term company resilience. The study adopts a conceptual and secondary-research method that draws on academic literature, sustainability frameworks, regulatory trends, management insights, and environmental performance, social responsibility, governance quality, stakeholder engagement, risk management and value creation. The paper suggests an integrated ESG–Corporate Strategy Framework, in which ESG aspects are integrated throughout the strategic process of diagnosis, materiality assessment, objective setting, resource allocation, operational implementation, performance measurement, disclosure and continuous improvement. The analysis suggests that the best NFT in the ESG integration process is an organization's transition from separate sustainability initiatives to embedding material ESG issues into fundamental business decisions and board oversight, investment planning, supply-chain management, innovation, human-capital practices, and performance indicators. The paper also addresses the key challenges to implementation, such as disparate ESG data, different metrics, short-term management pressure, greenwashing, lack of internal resources and challenges of reconciling various stakeholder demands. The need for credible and decision useful ESG information has further grown in importance in recent times with the developments in sustainability reporting. The paper argues that ESG should not be just a reporting tool, but a comprehensive management framework that is able to weave sustainability goals into a competitive positioning, organizational resilience, stakeholder legitimacy and long-term value creation.

title: Does Green Supply Chain Partnership Governance Pay Off? An Investigation of the Impact on Corporate Financial Performance
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines whether governance of green supply chain partnerships (GSCPs) using environmental criteria for supplier selection and termination is positively associated with corporate financial performance of focal firms. Drawing on the social capital theory, this study highlights the dichotomous nature of social capital in GSCPs, showing whether firms can gain corporate reputation and then financial benefits while proactively managing GSCPs. This study analysed the panel data of 994 firm‐year observations from UK FTSE All‐Share firms obtained from the Thomson Reuters Eikon's ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) database. Analysis result shows that although there is evidence that GSCP governance is positively related to corporate reputation, no evidence shows that corporate reputation will be a mediator between GSCP governance and corporate finance performance. Instead, GSCP governance variables have shown positive direct relationship with financial performance. Findings provide practical guidance for managers seeking to strengthen financial performance through GSCP governance approaches.

title: Managerial Innovation as a Lever for Digital Transformation Success: Toward an Integrated Organizational Value Creation Framework
summary: The accelerating pace of digital transformation has fundamentally restructured competitive landscapes across industries, compelling organizations to reconsider not only their technological investments but, more critically, their managerial architectures and innovation capacities. While extant scholarship has extensively examined the technological dimensions of digital transformation, comparatively limited attention has been devoted to managerial innovation as a primary enabling condition for sustained digital transformation success. This article addresses that gap by developing a theoretically grounded, integrative conceptual framework—the Integrated Organizational Value Creation Framework (IOVCF)—that articulates the causal pathways through which managerial innovation drives digital transformation and ultimately generates organizational value. Anchored in four complementary theoretical perspectives—Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the Resource-Based View (RBV), Organizational Change Theory, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory—the framework models a cascading logic: managerial innovation cultivates organizational capabilities (agility, learning, adaptability, and collaborative intelligence), which in turn facilitate digital transformation success (technology adoption, process digitalization, data integration, and digital innovation), culminating in multi-dimensional organizational value creation (operational performance, resilience, stakeholder satisfaction, and sustainable competitive advantage). Twelve formal research propositions are derived and theoretically justified. Managerial implications emphasize that digital transformation leaders must invest in organizational redesign, agile management practices, digital culture formation, knowledge management systems, employee empowerment, and collaborative ecosystems alongside—and often prior to—technology deployment. A rich agenda for future empirical research is outlined, encompassing cross-national validation, SME contexts, AI-enabled transformation, and sustainability-oriented digital strategies.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF SUPPLIER COLLABORATION: A CASE STUDY ON MIGRATING LEGACY SNC SYSTEM TO SAP BTP
summary: Digital transformation is increasingly critical for procurement organizations in asset intensive industries, where supplier responsiveness, logistics accuracy, and operational continuity are essential. This study examines the modernization of a legacy Supplier Network Collaboration (SNC) system within a major oil and gas enterprise through its migration to a unified DigitalSupplier platform. The legacy SNC environment suffered from fragmented workflows, limited mobility, redundant identity management processes, and restricted real time visibility, all of which negatively affected supplier onboarding and the accuracy of Advanced Shipping Notifications (ASNs). Using the SAP Activate methodology, the transformation introduced seven integrated SAP Fiori and SAP UI5 applications synchronized with SAP S/4HANA and supported by centralized master data governance. A 90 day parallel run was conducted to compare the performance of SNC and DigitalSupplier. The results demonstrate significant improvements: supplier onboarding time decreased from five working days to one hour, adoption increased by 40%, support tickets declined by 20%, and ASN errors were reduced by 10%. title: Bibliometric Analysis of Liquidity Dynamics of Islamic Commercial Banks in Indonesia: A Comprehensive Study of the Post-Pandemic Era
summary: This study aims to map the dynamics of the literature on the liquidity of Sharia commercial banks (BUS) in Indonesia during the post-pandemic transition period. The method used is bibliometric analysis by extracting data from the SINTA database, which is then visualized using VOSviewer software to identify trends, novelty, and Inter-variable connectivity. The results showed that there are four main discourse clusters, namely: risk management and financial performance, market structure and policy, monetary instruments and digital transformation and financial literacy. Key findings indicate that the resilience of post-pandemic BUS liquidity is strongly influenced by the strengthening of the capital buffer and the effectiveness of Islamic Corporate Governance (ICG) in reducing financing risks. The implications of this study provide a strategic foundation for regulators and banking practitioners in mitigating liquidity risk through third-party fund product innovation and strengthening digitization to deal with future economic volatility.

title: How Does the Digital Economy Drive County-Level Sustainable Development? A Perspective on the Coordinated Development of Economic and Environmental Resilience
summary: The digital economy is a vital engine driving grassroots sustainable development, yet whether and how it promotes the coordinated evolution of economic and environmental resilience at the county level remains to be further empirically tested. Using panel data for 1399 Chinese counties from 2018 to 2023, this study constructs an evaluation system for coordinated dual resilience based on the evolutionary framework of resistance, adaptability, and transformation, and measures digital economy development through word-frequency analysis of county government work reports. The baseline regression results show that the digital economy significantly promotes the coordinated development of county-level economic and environmental resilience, breaking the zero-sum game between grassroots economic growth and ecological protection. Mechanism tests reveal a bidirectional driving pathway of industry and society: the digital economy not only exerts an industrial driving effect by empowering advanced productive forces and increasing the level of industrial agglomeration, but also plays a social reshaping role by enhancing talent retention potential and improving social service effectiveness. Heterogeneity analysis further indicates that this synergistic effect is stronger in southern counties and in counties covered by the Comprehensive Demonstration Program for E-commerce in Rural Areas. By shifting the sustainable development perspective to the micro-level of counties, this study provides practical policy implications for formulating differentiated, targeted digital investment strategies and optimizing the supply of grassroots digital public goods.

title: Technostress in the age of digital transformation and AI: A bibliometric–systematic literature review for HRM research
summary: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are reshaping human resource management through algorithmic recruitment, automated evaluation, predictive analytics, and generative tools. While these systems improve efficiency, they also intensify technostress through opacity, surveillance, reduced control, and digitally intensified work arrangements. Responding to a fragmented literature spanning both AI-enabled and broader digital work systems, this study provides a B-SLR that maps technostress in digital transformation while identifying AI-specific stressors as a key emerging stream for HRM research. Drawing on 194 Scopus-indexed articles, we combine performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, dominant themes, and intellectual structures. The review shows how AI-specific stressors extend established technostress mechanisms and shift attention toward transparency, control, fairness, and responsible HRM design. We conclude with actionable implications for researchers and practitioners aiming to design more transparent, responsible, and sustainable digital and AI-enabled HRM systems.

title: Digital Transformation for Accounting Students in Facing the Development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the World of Accounting
summary: The development of digital transformation and Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has brought significant changes in the world of accounting, especially in the process of recording transactions, preparing financial statements, digital audits, and fraud detection. This research aims to analyze digital transformation for accounting students in facing the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the world of accounting. The research method used is Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with a thematic synthesis approach to scientific articles obtained from Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, ResearchGate, and Scopus for the 2024–2026 period. Of the 80 articles found, 15 articles that met the inclusion criteria were obtained and analyzed further. The results of the study show that digital transformation has a major impact on the accounting profession with the increasing use of accounting software, cloud computing, blockchain, and AI in business processes. Accounting students are required not only to understand accounting theory, but also to have digital competencies such as mastery of accounting information systems, data analysis, and the use of AI-based technology. Factors that affect students' readiness to face AI include digital literacy, educational curriculum, technology access, and adaptability. In addition to presenting challenges in the form of increasing job competition and the need for technology skills, AI also opens up new opportunities in the accounting profession such as digital auditors, financial data analysts, and information systems consultants. Therefore, universities need to update the curriculum to be more relevant to technological developments and industrial needs in the digital era.
