title: Life Cycle Assessment of Virgin and Recycled Polypropylene Kitchenware in the UK: Impacts of Domestic Recycling, International Supply Chains, and Consumer Use
summary: This study evaluates the cradle-to-grave environmental performance of polypropylene (PP) kitchenware in the United Kingdom (UK), addressing critical gaps in understanding how material choices, global supply chains, domestic recycling, and consumer use-phase practices interact. Four scenarios were assessed using life cycle assessment (LCA) modelling: virgin PP (vPP) manufactured in China and Germany, recycled PP (rPP) produced in the UK, and a 50:50 vPP–rPP blend. Environmental impacts evaluated using the ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) and IPCC 2021 GWP100 showed that under the modelled scenarios, UK-produced rPP reduces global warming potential (GWP) by about 53% compared with imported vPP, and by 22% compared with UK-manufactured vPP from Germany, driven by avoided virgin polymer production, the absence of long-distance shipping and end-of-life recycling. Toxicity-related impacts revealed trade-offs associated with recycling processes. The rPP product reduced terrestrial ecotoxicity and human non-carcinogenic toxicity by approximately 36% and 16% relative to imported vPP, demonstrating rPP’s potential to reduce toxicity-related impacts. Consumer use-phase practices (routine household dishwashing) contributed substantially to lifecycle impacts, becoming the dominant life cycle stage (30-64% of GWP) as material-related impacts were reduced. The study demonstrates that the environmental performance of consumer plastics requires integrated consideration of material systems efficiency, geography, supply-chain arrangements, recycling infrastructure, and consumer behaviour. Such an approach can promote circularity in polymer value chains, with the potential to generate substantial environmental, economic, technical and social benefits.

title: Tax planning, ESG disclosure, and firm value: Does ESG act as a reputational buffer? Evidence from consumer goods firms
summary: This study examines the effect of tax planning on firm value, viewed as the market's assessment of reputational capital, and the moderating role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosure. Two competing predictions are tested: ESG disclosure acts as a reputational buffer that mitigates market penalties for tax planning, or it amplifies those penalties by signalling inconsistency. The sample comprises 10 branded consumer goods manufacturers listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange over 2022–2024 (30 firm-year observations). Tax planning is measured by the Cash Effective Tax Rate (CETR), ESG disclosure by a GRI Standards-based disclosure index, and firm value by the natural logarithm of Tobin's Q. Moderated regression with mean-centred variables and firm-clustered standard errors is employed. The results show that CETR is positively associated with firm value, implying that firms with more intensive tax planning tend to be valued lower; however, this association is significant only at the 10% level and is not robust to firm fixed effects. ESG disclosure has no direct effect and does not moderate the relationship, so neither the buffer nor the amplifier hypothesis is supported. The findings suggest that the market does not yet use the breadth of ESG disclosure to assess corporate tax behaviour, underscoring the need for explicit tax transparency.

title: Abaddon, Apollyon, and the Signature of the Destroyer: Toward a Biblical-Theological Diagnostic for Destructive Leadership, Intangible Capital Liquidation, and Corporate Governance in Emerging Markets
summary: This paper, authored by Dr. Ohio O. Ojeagbase (FICA, S.FIDR) of the Kreeno Consortium and the Kreeno Centre for Debt Recovery and Cognitive Governance Institute, Lagos, addresses a critical blind spot in corporate governance research—namely, the failure of conventional financial metrics to detect the systematic liquidation of intangible capital (relational trust, epistemic integrity, and regulatory goodwill) that is often masked by short-term financial vitality. Drawing on precise lexical-semantic analysis of biblical destruction terminology (Hebrew *sātan*, Greek *diabolos*, *ho kleptēs* of John 10:10, and *Abaddon/Apollyon* of Revelation 9:11) combined with abductive thematic synthesis, the paper constructs a four-stage "Signature of the Destroyer" morphology—counterfeit illumination, the Judas archetype of relational liquidation, intangible asset conversion, and eventual self-perpetuating collapse (Abaddon unleashed)—which it then operationalizes into a 16-item Fiduciary Diagnostic Matrix (covering Epistemic Transparency, Risk Asymmetry, Relational Resilience, and Post-Tenure Viability) for boardroom use. Grounded in an illustrative composite case from the Nigerian microfinance sector (2019–2023), the paper offers a hermeneutically disciplined, theologically anchored alternative to secular toxic-leadership models, arguing that fiduciary stewardship is a covenantal duty and that the highest calling of leadership is not maximum extraction but the preservation of what must never be sacrificed—human dignity, truthfulness, and intergenerational stability.

title: Harmonizing Economic Governance and Constitutional Values: A Study of Compliance under SEBI, Competition, Tax, and Anti-Money Laundering Laws
summary: This paper shows how a growing sense of justice among ordinary people forms a complex yet coherent framework of harmonious construction that ties modern Corporate Governance to the Indian Constitution. It firmly contends that the sword of Damocles in the Indian Constitution, a powerful means of piercing the corporate veil in major corporate governance failures, is inconsistent with Articles 14, 19 and 21, and is therefore 'not' fair, just, reasonable, fundamentally right and non-Arbitrary. In other words, mala fide intentions must override corporate governance norms to preserve the conscience of the Preamble's sanctity within the Constitution of India; otherwise, the exact opposite will be treated as a corporate governance statute or policy under Article 13(2) and the Doctrine of Severability, as curtailing public policy and posing a major threat that causes gross irritation within the lines of natural justice. It broadly surveys these substantive statutes as one manifesto of 'how': the SEBI Act, the Competition Act, the Income Tax Act and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) all fit the Indian Constitution's provisions on the substantive law of economic regulation, which seeks to fulfil the state's mandate under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), Article 39(b) and (c), to stop wealth from concentrating in a few hands. That policy is ultimately inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights to Equality and to Freedom of Trade and Commerce in Part III of the Constitution of India. By exposing glaring corporate governance failures, this study shows how routinely enforcement agencies upgrade de minimis procedural and disclosure defaults into white-collar crimes, peeling away the cosy veil of procedural double jeopardy in corporate law matters and thereby violating Article 14's ban on Arbitrariness, Article 19(1)(g)'s Right to Trade and Commerce, Article 20(3)'s protection against self-Incrimination, and the substantive due process protection during searches, seizures and attachments under Article 21. This study closes by proposing three novel statutory remedies: 1. Adoption of the "Lead Regulator Doctrine"; 2. Implementation of a Protected Foreign Quote that blocks criminal asset freezes by regulators until the underlying disputes are resolved; and 3. "Proportionality Audits" of new norms notified by SEBI. In the end, this study argues that market governance and freedoms are not mutually exclusive but are both essential pillars of a healthy economy, and it therefore advocates their harmonious coexistence as two sides of the same coin.

title: Stakeholder influence in sustainable tourism under digital transformation through an integrated Delphi, AHP and DEMATEL framework
summary: Abstract This study examines stakeholder influence in Vietnam’s national sustainable tourism governance system under digital transformation. Although stakeholder roles are widely recognized, limited research has distinguished perceived importance from expert-assessed directional influence within digitally mediated governance systems. Drawing on judgments from 18 Vietnamese experts, the study integrates a two-round Delphi process to validate six stakeholder groups and twelve sub-factors, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to estimate their relative importance, and the Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) to assess directional interdependencies among the six stakeholder groups. The results reveal a notable divergence between stakeholder importance and directional influence. Central Government ranks first in AHP and occupies the strongest net-influencing position. Tourism Enterprises rank second and exhibit the highest systemic prominence but occupy an effect-oriented position, indicating high systemic involvement while receiving more overall influence than they exert. Knowledge and Research Institutions receive the lowest AHP weight yet occupy a net-influencing position. Local Government is also classified within the net-influencing group, whereas Local Communities and Tourists occupy effect-oriented positions. These findings demonstrate that stakeholder importance, systemic prominence, and net influence do not necessarily coincide. The study extends stakeholder salience research by incorporating a relational, system-level perspective and conceptualizes digital transformation as a governance-embedded coordination mechanism rather than an autonomous driver of sustainability. It provides policy-relevant insights for strengthening institutional coordination, knowledge support, stakeholder participation, and sustainable tourism governance.

title: INVENTORY MATERIALITY DETERMINATION AND AUDITOR’S OPINION
summary: Our study explores the significance of materiality levels in inventory audits and their influence on independent auditors’ opinions, a crucial aspect of financial reporting and decision-making. Specifically, our study investigates how factors such as gender, age, education level, audit experience, and the number of files audited influence materiality assessment, audit planning, participation in audit techniques, and ultimately, auditors’ opinions on inventory audits. We employ an online survey methodology, targeting auditors from firms authorized by the Public Oversight Authority in Istanbul. Our findings reveal notable variations in audit practices, particularly regarding materiality levels, audit approaches, planning strategies, and inventory auditing techniques. Furthermore, incorrect materiality assessments appear to contribute to inaccurate audit opinions, underlining the importance of precise evaluation methods. Finally, the techniques applied in inventory auditing play a crucial role in shaping auditors’ final conclusions.

title: Effect of Fintech Adoption on Customer Retention in Deposit Money Banks in Wukari Metropolis
summary: This study examined the effect of Fintech Adoption on Customer Retention in selected Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) in Wukari Metropolis, Taraba State. The research was necessitated by the increasing "churn rate" of traditional bank customers toward aggressive Fintech rivals (Neo-banks) despite heavy investments in digital infrastructure by DMBs. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised active digital banking customers of three selected active DMBs in Wukari, including, UBA, Zenith Bank, and Unity Bank. A sample size of 300 respondents was determined using convenience sampling. Data were collected using a structured 4-point Likert scale questionnaire, validated by experts, and tested for reliability using Cronbach’s Alpha, which yielded a coefficient of 0.84. Data analysis was performed using descriptive statistics and Multiple Regression Analysis via SPSS Version 27. Findings revealed that while Payment Channels (USSD and Mobile Apps) significantly drive usage frequency, Settlement Infrastructure (ATM and POS uptime) emerged as the most critical factor influencing long-term loyalty and advocacy in the Wukari Metropolis (beta = 0.412, p < 0.05). Furthermore, Security Architecture was found to be the primary driver of switching resistance among the community. The study concluded that Fintech adoption is a significant predictor of customer retention.

title: Entrepreneurial Performance and Sustainable Entrepreneurship: A Review of Psychological, Individual, Organisational and Environmental Determinants
summary: Entrepreneurial performance is a multidimensional phenomenon that is influenced by the psychological attributes, individual competencies, organisational capabilities, financial resources, technological developments and environment. This is crucial for fostering entrepreneurship effectiveness and sustainable entrepreneurship development as these determinants are interrelated. The key factors affecting the performance of entrepreneurs are explored, focusing on emotional intelligence, entrepreneurial orientation, education, the digital transformation, financial capabilities, institutional support and sustainability. The review brings together literature on psychological and individual factors, entrepreneurial orientation and competency building, digital transformation and financial skills, as well as environmental, institutional and sustainable entrepreneurship. The reviewed studies have identified emotional intelligence as a salient psychological factor that facilitates emotional control, making decisions, coping with adversity, interpersonal relationships, leadership, and flexibility in the face of unpredictable business environments. The other factors that contribute to opportunity recognition, innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and venture development are entrepreneurial education, experiential learning, digital competencies and entrepreneurial orientation. Digital technologies and artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital platforms and other technologies offer opportunities to enhance resource mobilisation, market access and organisational performance, but face issues of digital inequality, ethical governance and technological capacity. Entrepreneurial development and the ability to embrace sustainable business practices are also affected by financial literacy, access to finance, saving patterns and green finance.

title: Machine Learning Utilisation and Perceived Financial Reporting Quality among Employees of Selected Listed Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria: A PLS-SEM Analysis
summary: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in accounting and assurance processes, yet focused evidence on its relationship with financial reporting quality (FRQ) in Nigerian banking remains limited. This study examines the association between ML utilisation and perceived FRQ among employees of selected listed Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) in Nigeria. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was used. The study population comprised 243 eligible employees; 181 questionnaires were distributed after allowing for anticipated non-response, 151 completed questionnaires were returned, and all 151 were valid for analysis, yielding a response rate of 83.43%. ML and perceived FRQ were measured with five indicators each on a five-point Likert scale. PLS-SEM was implemented in SmartPLS 4. The measurement model demonstrated strong indicator loadings, reliability, and convergent validity, although the very high reliability coefficients warrant assessment of possible item redundancy. ML utilisation was positively associated with perceived FRQ (β = 0.719, t = 12.63, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.631, 0.788]). The model explained 51.7% of the variance in perceived FRQ (R² = 0.517; adjusted R² = 0.514), with a large effect size (f² = 1.07). Because the design is cross-sectional and perception-based, the findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The study contributes focused evidence on ML utilisation and perceived financial-reporting quality in the Nigerian listed-banking context.

title: Beyond continuance: how FinTech app experiences shape user well-being
summary: Purpose This study examines how users' everyday experiences with digital wallet apps, as a major category of FinTech applications, shape their well-being rather than focusing only on continued use. Using real user reviews from Saudi Arabia, it identifies four key experiential factors: complaint handling effectiveness, perceived system reliability, information ambiguity, and user autonomy. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the study explains how these factors shape user well-being. Design/methodology/approach We applied a sequential mixed-methods design guided by Computational User Feedback Analytics (CUFA) to Arabic and English reviews collected from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store. CUFA integrates hierarchical clustering, Latent Dirichlet Allocation( topic modeling, sentiment analysis, multi-model classification, human validation, and regularized regression. We interpreted the review-derived constructs through SDT and tested them using Ridge and Lasso regression. Findings Our findings indicate that complaint handling effectiveness, perceived system reliability, and user autonomy positively shape user well-being. In contrast, information ambiguity negatively affects user well-being. Originality/value Unlike prior studies that rely predominantly on structured surveys and predefined adoption models, this study applies CUFA to derive, validate, and test theoretically meaningful constructs using large-scale, unsolicited user feedback. It also extends SDT into the fintech context by showing how specific digital wallet experiences support or frustrate users' psychological needs.

title: Квантитативна процена нивоа транспарентности ЕSG извештавања у индустријском сектору
summary: This paper presents a quantitative assessment of the transparency of ESG reporting in the industrial sector. The analysis is based on publicly available ESG reports and applies a scorecard model with four criteria: usage of standardized ESG frameworks, external verification, quantified sustainability targets, and clearly defined key performance indicators (KPIs) with a base year. The study focuses on environmental indicators such as greenhouse gas emissions, energy and water usage, and waste management. The results show clear differences between international and domestic companies, with firms in the EU regulatory framework ESRS demonstrating higher transparency and methodological consistency. The findings suggest that standardized reporting frameworks and external verification improve the credibility and comparability of ESG disclosures.

title: The implications of student personality types for excellent teaching in accounting higher education: A systematic literature review
summary: Prior research suggests that personality plays an important role in shaping accounting students' learning and professional development. This study synthesises 83 empirical articles published between 1972 and 2024 that examine the role of personality in accounting education. Using the Antecedents–Decisions–Outcomes (ADO) framework, the SPAR-4-SLR protocol, the PICOS search tool, and the PRISMA reporting flow, the study draws on Scopus and ABDC-listed journals. The thematic analysis identifies six key areas through which personality influences accounting students: personality dynamics, academic performance, accounting careers, ethical behaviour, professional behaviour, and entrepreneurship. Based on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual framework and personality-based pedagogical strategies to support teaching excellence. Specifically, the study recommends three teaching strategies: a balanced personality approach to financial accounting, a structured analytical transition to management accounting, and a practical scepticism approach to auditing. The present study also highlights the lack of research on personality in the tax profession or tax courses, which could guide future researchers.

title: AI-driven whole-life costing for decision-ready UK public building retrofits
summary: Abstract Public-sector building retrofits in the United Kingdom require decisions that balance whole-life cost, carbon reduction, service continuity and auditability under limited data and constrained capital budgets. This paper develops a decision-ready whole-life costing (WLC) workflow that integrates environmental, social and governance (ESG) priorities with uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence (AI) for public-building retrofit appraisal. The workflow combines national non-domestic Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and Display Energy Certificate (DEC) data, Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) delivery evidence and stakeholder inputs to construct a scenario library of public-building archetypes, retrofit actions and appraisal constraints. Stakeholder priorities from interviews, a questionnaire and a co-design workshop are translated into transparent weights using fuzzy analytic hierarchy process (F-AHP). These weights parameterise a reinforcement learning (RL) planner, while a Bayesian convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (BCNN–LSTM) surrogate provides uncertainty-bounded energy, carbon and cost trajectories for repeated policy evaluation. Results show that the workflow supports auditable retrofit sequencing across archetype and budget conditions and improves composite ESG performance relative to conventional WLC-only, £/tCO 2 e and static multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) baselines. For 1000 matched archetype–budget cases, the trained deep Q-network (DQN) decision-search stage achieves a 30.03-fold speedup over traditional scalar feasible-sequence enumeration. The contribution is an integrated and explainable WLC–ESG–AI workflow for early-stage public retrofit decision support. The current validation remains based on public datasets and scenario-level evidence so future work should extend the framework using project-specific metered data, digital twins and live portfolio deployment.

title: EXTRATERRITORIAL DUE DILIGENCE: THE IMPACT OF THE EU CORPORATE SUSTAINABILITY DIRECTIVE ON INDIAN LABOUR COMPLIANCE
summary: The European Union (EU) Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) has transformed transnational corporate governance and domestic labour compliance. This paper discusses in detail the legal, economic and operational conflicts resulting from the extraterritorial application of the CSDDD to the Indian manufacturing and textile industries. The European parent companies have, in effect, codified international standards of human rights and environmental due diligence throughout their global chains of activities. This has created friction with the Indian suppliers whose primary regulations and standards include the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, and the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. Thus, these regulations and standards are thus subject to European compliance enforcement through private contracts, with all the implications of civil liability under the CSDDD and the "audit fatigue" amongst the Indian suppliers and the broader geo-political decisions for the Global South covered by this paper, that is, regulatory domination.

summary: This research studies developers’ affordable housing strategies, driving factors for participation in the Million Housing Project (2018–2024), and operational outcomes. Using a mixed-methods design, data were gathered from corporate documents and interviews with executives from four case study including SET-listed and Non-SET companies. The Analysis was guided by CSR/ESG, subsidy, and credit underwriting frameworks. The study findings reveal that 1) entrepreneurs view affordable housing development as a business opportunity coupled with corporate social responsibility, whereby listed companies participate liquidate their existing inventory, while half of non-listed companies apply for loans to develop new projects and the other half bring already-developed projects into the program; 2) listed companies are driven by corporate vision and internal expertise, whereas non-listed companies prioritize local market factors, with limited purchasing power and household debt serving as shared external constraints; 3) participation enhances their image sustainability, through which listed companies can effectively accelerate cash flow, while non-listed companies gain publicity and some can reduce their financial costs through project development loans; however, high loan rejection rates and selling price caps remain major limitations. Strategically, the government must move beyond financial incentives to integrate, non-financial support. Relaxing zoning regulations and land subdivision laws are necessary to facilitate budget development. Additionally, expanding public infrastructure near industrial hubs is essential to lower supply-side costs. sustainably incentivizing continuous private investment.

title: PENGARUH SISTEM INFORMASI AKUNTANSI, KOMPETENSI SUMBER DAYA MANUSIA, DAN PENGENDALIAN INTERNAL TERHADAP KUALITAS LAPORAN KEUANGAN PADA BALAI PEMASYARAKATAN KELAS IIA KOTA KUPANG
summary: This study examines the effects of accounting information systems, human resource competence, and internal control on financial reporting quality at the Class IIA Correctional Center in Kupang. A quantitative descriptive-associative approach was applied to 42 employees involved in financial administration and reporting. Data were collected through questionnaires, interviews, observations, and documentation and analyzed using multiple linear regression in SPSS. Accounting information systems (t = 2.575; p = 0.014), human resource competence (t = 2.335; p = 0.025), and internal control (t = 2.483; p = 0.018) were each positively and significantly associated with financial reporting quality. The joint model was significant (F = 32.064; p < 0.001), with R² = 0.717. These findings underscore the importance of combining reliable accounting systems, capable personnel, and effective controls to improve public-sector financial reporting. The single-institution design limits generalization.

title: Forensic Accounting Literacy and Accounting Students’ Perceptions of Fraud Prevention in Makassar City: A Literature Review
summary: Fraud is an important issue for accounting education because students are expected not only to understand financial recording and reporting, but also to recognize irregularities, evaluate evidence, and uphold professional integrity. This article examines the relationship between forensic accounting literacy, accounting students' perceptions, and fraud prevention, while positioning Makassar City as the setting for the educational implications of the review. A literature review method is employed through narrative-thematic synthesis of empirical studies that address forensic accounting knowledge and skills, fraud awareness, fraud literacy, fraud detection capability, and fraud prevention strategies. The synthesis indicates that knowledge, analytical ability, professional skepticism, anti-fraud awareness, and investigative techniques tend to strengthen individuals' readiness to identify fraud risks and support preventive action. Evidence also shows that knowledge does not always translate directly into anti-fraud behavior because its effect may depend on motivation, professional skepticism, ethical conditions, and control systems. For accounting students in Makassar City, the findings highlight the value of forensic accounting education that combines conceptual understanding with case analysis, red-flag identification, investigative exercises, ethics, and communication of findings. The review offers a conceptual basis for universities to strengthen anti-fraud education and provides a foundation for future survey research that measures students' perceptions directly

title: ESG Reliability Post‐Paris Agreement: Evidence From S&P 500 Firms
summary: ABSTRACT This research investigates whether the 2015 Paris Agreement has changed environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance scores. We compiled a balanced panel of 392 S&P 500 companies from 2010 to 2025 using Refinitiv data. The final dataset contained 6272 observations on the 10 ESG scores at the most detailed level possible. Based on stakeholder theory, interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) was applied to determine whether the intercorrelations among the ESG variables decreased post‐Paris. Moreover, in accordance with legitimacy theory, the reported ESG measures were examined using Benford's law. It was found that the uniformity of the last digits improved over time. Three robustness checks were carried out: (a) an out‐of‐sample ITSA with 293 STOXX‐listed companies, (b) a quadratic ITSA, and (c) placebo tests with different breakpoints. The evidence indicates (1) the downward trend became stronger in the period after the Paris Agreement and (2) the differentiation among ESG scores accelerated in a nonlinear manner. We conclude the reliability of ESG performance scores has increased over time, providing a more trustworthy foundation for stakeholders' decision‐making.
